doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Future standards and approach to songs
summary: Who is writing future standards, the Sondheim album, a standard's definition, and how much liberty they take.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Do you think there’s anybody writing tunes today that are going to become standards? © Fillius Jazz Archive -30-
Johnny Mandel is writing some gorgeous things.

Dave Frishberg writes interesting things. Who else? There must be others. Well people like Gerry Mulligan have written classics but they’re not songs with lyrics so I don’t know. But there’ll be standard classic jazz pieces, you know, just like his “Line for Lyons” and “Boplicity,” and those things are gorgeous. They’ll always sound good. And Gil Evans things, and who else, I don’t know, Miles.
Any of the show tunes perhaps?

There are some. I mean some of Sondheim’s things are very nice. We did a Sondheim album and we never thought we could do it because we always felt that they didn’t lend themselves to jazz that well. And some of them don’t as much as others. So we found some that we thought worked fairly well for us, and it turned out pretty good. We liked it.
I wanted to read something you said. “A standard has chords that are familiar to anyone, yet interesting enough to the performer to encourage a serious approach.”

Well you take the sheet music and some of it is great. Hey that’s a good beginning. And then you do a little alteration, and do this and that, and make something that satisfies the inner self. It makes it interesting.

And you know usually when we do a standard or something that people know, we try to honor it the way the composer wrote it, I mean pretty much so. You know you try to sing the melody the way — the right notes he wanted and the right chords. But then if it’s a song that’s really been used a lot and done by a lot of people, then we feel we can take more liberty. They’ve heard it that way. They’ve heard it that way a thousand times, and now we can start out and maybe do it a little differently, maybe change a note here or a chord there.
